nameStory: Despite its name, marsh marigold isn't actually a marigold at all! The 'marigold' part comes from the golden-yellow flowers that reminded early settlers of true marigolds, while 'marsh' perfectly describes where you'll find this wetland-loving plant. Its other common name, kingcup, refers to the cup-shaped flowers that seemed fit for royalty.
description: Marsh marigold is a cheerful wetland wildflower that brightens up soggy spots with brilliant golden-yellow blooms in spring and early summer. This low-growing perennial plant typically reaches 1-2 feet tall and spreads in patches along stream edges and wet meadows. Its shiny, heart-shaped leaves and bright buttercup-like flowers make it one of the most recognizable plants in New England's wetlands. The whole plant has a succulent, watery feel that helps it thrive in constantly moist conditions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers with 5-9 glossy, petal-like sepals that shine like they've been polished with butter. The flowers are about 1-2 inches across and have no true petals - what looks like petals are actually sepals that do the showoff work.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, kidney or heart-shaped leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch. They're bright green and glossy, often with scalloped or rounded edges, and grow on long stalks directly from the base of the plant.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low clumps or patches in wet areas, with flowers and leaves emerging directly from the ground on separate stalks. The plant has a dense, bushy appearance when in full bloom.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Hollow, succulent stems that feel thick and juicy when gently squeezed. They're smooth and often have a slightly reddish tinge at the base.

habitat: Look for marsh marigold in New England's wettest spots - along stream banks, in marshy meadows, around pond edges, and in wet woodlands where water seeps or stands. It thrives in rich, mucky soils that stay constantly moist and can tolerate partial shade under wet woodland canopies. You'll often find it growing alongside skunk cabbage, wild leeks, and other moisture-loving spring wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: This is marsh marigold's time to shine! Bright golden flowers appear from April through May, creating stunning displays in wet areas just as trees are leafing out.
seasonality.summer: Flowers may continue into early summer in cooler, higher elevation sites. Leaves remain green and prominent throughout the summer months, forming attractive foliage patches.
seasonality.fall: Leaves gradually die back and turn brown as temperatures drop. Seeds mature and disperse during this time.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground parts, leaving little trace above ground until spring's return.

funFact: Marsh marigold flowers are actually solar panels in disguise - their glossy petals act like tiny mirrors that focus extra warmth toward the center of the flower, creating a cozy landing pad that attracts cold spring insects and helps the plant's reproductive parts develop faster in chilly weather!
confusionNotes: Marsh marigold is most likely confused with other yellow spring wildflowers, but its wetland habitat is the biggest clue - if your feet aren't getting wet, you're probably not looking at marsh marigold! The thick, waxy leaves and hollow stems also set it apart from drier-ground yellow flowers like buttercups.
contextualKnowledge: Like many members of the buttercup family, marsh marigold contains compounds that make it toxic when raw, though some indigenous peoples traditionally cooked the young leaves as a spring green after multiple water changes to remove the bitter, harmful substances.
compareHints: As the only Caltha species commonly found in New England, marsh marigold is most similar to other buttercup family members like regular buttercups and lesser celandine. However, marsh marigold's much larger size, wetland habitat, and thick succulent leaves easily distinguish it from the smaller, drier-ground buttercups with their more delicate, divided leaves.
